a: Do not break down before them, or I will break you down in front of them.
p: The Hebrew warns Jeremiah; the Greek gives him a promise of rescue.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); the Hebrew text on which the Plain English is built
readings.orig: אַל תֵּחַת מִפְּנֵיהֶם פֶּן אֲחִתְּךָ לִפְנֵיהֶם
readings.en: Do not be shattered before them, or I will shatter you before them.
readings.plain: Do not break down before them, or I will break you down in front of them.

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: μὴ φοβηθῇς ἀπὸ προσώπου αὐτῶν μηδὲ πτοηθῇς ἐναντίον αὐτῶν, ὅτι μετὰ σοῦ εἰμὶ τοῦ ἐξαιρεῖσθαί σε, λέγει Κύριος
readings.en: Do not be afraid of them or terrified before them, for I am with you to rescue you, says the Lord.
readings.plain: Do not be afraid of them or terrified in front of them, for I am with you to pull you free, the LORD declares.

why: The Hebrew is the harder reading and has a pointed wordplay on 'shatter'. The Greek's ending, 'for I am with you to rescue you', copies the promise of 1:8 and 1:19 and may have been brought in to smooth the line, though it could also come from a Hebrew text without the threat.
b: No Qumran scroll preserves this verse, so there is no early Hebrew witness besides the Masoretic Text. The Greek has no 'lest I shatter you'. Commentators divide on which text is older.

a: an iron pillar, and walls of bronze
t: Pillar and walls, or one wall?
p: The Greek has the fortified city and a bronze wall, but no iron pillar.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and an iron pillar and walls of bronze
readings.plain: an iron pillar, and walls of bronze

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition): 'like a fortified city and like a bronze wall'
readings.orig: ὡς πόλιν ὀχυρὰν καὶ ὡς τεῖχος χαλκοῦν
readings.en: like a fortified city and like a bronze wall
readings.plain: and a wall of bronze

why: The Hebrew lists a fortified city, an iron pillar and bronze walls, a build-up of three pictures. The Greek has the city and a bronze wall, and no pillar; its shorter list may be the earlier form, or the pillar may have dropped out. The later book repeats the Hebrew's 'fortified wall of bronze' (15:20). No scroll preserves 1:18.

a: its priests and
t: The priests are not in the Greek list
p: The Greek lists the kings, officials and people but not the priests.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and its priests
readings.plain: its priests and

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.en: (omitted)

why: Jeremiah was himself a priest, and the Hebrew list makes the priests among his opponents, as the rest of the book does (20:1-2; 26:7-8). The Greek could have dropped them or the Hebrew could have added them.

a: The word of the LORD came to me:
p: The Greek omits the verse; it goes with 2:2.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: The word of the LORD came to me:
readings.plain: The word of the LORD came to me:

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition): no 2:1
readings.en: (nothing)

why: The introduction is typical Jeremiah style and no Hebrew witness lacks it. The Greek's shorter text starts the speech with 'And he said'. This goes together with the next entry.
b: No scroll of Jeremiah preserves 2:1-2, so only the Greek is known as a witness for the shorter text here. If the Greek reflects an earlier Hebrew, this is one of the book's headings that was added in the longer edition.

a: Go and call out in the ears of Jerusalem.
t: 'Go and call out' is missing in the Greek
p: The Greek omits the command to go and cry out in the ears of Jerusalem; this goes with 2:1.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: Go and call out in the ears of Jerusalem.
readings.plain: Go and call out in the ears of Jerusalem.

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.en: And he said, Thus says the Lord

why: The longer Hebrew has the sense of a public proclamation to the city, which suits what follows; no manuscript lacks it in Hebrew, but the Greek may reflect an earlier edition.

a: walked after me in the wilderness
t: 'After me in the wilderness' or 'after the Holy One of Israel'
p: The Greek has Israel follow 'the Holy One of Israel' and has no wilderness; it goes with the next entry.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: your walking after me in the wilderness
readings.plain: walked after me in the wilderness

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.en: your following the Holy One of Israel
readings.plain: followed the Holy One of Israel

why: The Hebrew has the LORD speaking in the first person and pictures the wilderness years, as Hosea 2:14-15 and Jeremiah 2:6 do. In the Greek the LORD is spoken of in the third person, 'the Holy One of Israel', which may be a translator's variation or a different Hebrew. Both texts have the wilderness in 2:6. No scroll preserves 2:2.
b: The Greek verse also begins 'And he said, Thus says the Lord' (see the entry at 2:2 above) and has 'love of its completion' where the Hebrew has 'the love of your engagement'.

a: in a land where nothing was sown
t: 'A land not sown' is not in the Greek
p: The Greek has no line about the unsown land; it goes with the entry before.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: in a land not sown
readings.plain: in a land where nothing was sown

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.en: (omitted)

why: The line balances 'in the wilderness' and matches the description of the wilderness in 2:6. The Greek's shorter verse may be a translator's cut or an earlier Hebrew. No scroll preserves 2:2.

a: will crush your skull
t: Crush your skull, or know and mock you?
p: The Greek has Memphis and Tahpanhes 'know you and mock you'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: will break (or graze) your scalp
readings.plain: will crush your skull

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.en: knew you and mocked you
readings.plain: knew you and mocked you

why: The Hebrew verb is hard (see the note), but 'crush your skull' fits Egypt as the power that hurt Judah. The Greek may have read the verb as 'know' (the Hebrew letters daleth and resh look alike) and has no word for 'skull'. It also asks, 'Did not this happen to you because you left me?', which the Hebrew has at the start of 2:17. No scroll preserves 2:16.

a: while he was leading you on the road
t: 'While he was leading you' is not in the Greek
p: The Greek has the question but not the clause about the LORD leading Israel on the road.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: when he was leading you on the way
readings.plain: while he was leading you on the road

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.en: (omitted)

why: The clause adds the thought that Judah left the LORD in the very act of being led by him, which is Jeremiah's usual language (compare 2:6). A Greek translator or his source could have dropped it, but it could also be an expansion in the longer Hebrew; no scroll preserves the verse.

a: I will not serve
p: The written Hebrew says 'serve'; the marginal reading says 'cross over' or 'transgress'.

readings.w: Ketiv (written) of the Leningrad Codex; Greek ('I will not serve you'); the sense of the yoke in the verse
readings.en: I will not serve
readings.plain: I will not serve

readings.w: Qere (read) of the Leningrad Codex
readings.en: I will not transgress
readings.plain: I will not cross over

why: Serving fits the yoke and straps that were broken in the line before. The Greek agrees with the written text, so two independent witnesses (the consonants of the Hebrew and the Greek) stand against the Qere. No scroll preserves this verse.
b: The Qere may have arisen because 'I will not serve' could be read as an oath of rebellion against the LORD.

a: and your throat from thirst.
p: The written text has 'threshing floor'; the margin and the Greek have 'throat'.

readings.w: Qere (read) of the Leningrad Codex; Greek ('throat')
readings.en: and your throat
readings.plain: and your throat from thirst.

readings.w: Ketiv (written) of the Leningrad Codex
readings.en: and your threshing floor
readings.plain: and your threshing floor from thirst.

why: 'Throat' goes with 'thirst', and the Greek agrees. 'Threshing floor' makes no sense beside 'thirst' and is probably a slip in which two letters changed places. The Greek also has 'rough road' where the Hebrew has 'barefoot'. No scroll preserves 2:25.

a: You gave birth to us
t: 'You gave birth to us' or 'to me'
p: The written text and the Greek say 'me'; the margin says 'us'.

readings.w: Qere (read) of the Leningrad Codex
readings.en: you gave birth to us
readings.plain: You gave birth to us

readings.w: Ketiv (written) of the Leningrad Codex; Greek ('you gave birth to me')
readings.en: you gave birth to me
readings.plain: You gave birth to me

why: The witnesses are split: the written text and the Greek have 'me', which goes with 'my father' in the line before. The Plain English keeps the margin's 'us' as the reading of the Masoretic tradition, and because a whole people is speaking; the sense is the same either way. No scroll preserves 2:27.

a: is the number of your gods, Judah.
t: A second line about Jerusalem's streets
p: The Greek adds that for each of Jerusalem's streets they sacrificed to Baal.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.orig: כִּי מִסְפַּר עָרֶיךָ הָיוּ אֱלֹהֶיךָ יְהוּדָה
readings.en: for as many as your cities were your gods, Judah
readings.plain: is the number of your gods, Judah.

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: καὶ κατ᾽ ἀριθμὸν διόδων τῆς Ἰερουσαλὴμ ἔθυον τῇ Βάαλ
readings.en: and according to the number of the streets of Jerusalem they sacrificed to Baal
readings.plain: is the number of your gods, Judah, and for each of Jerusalem's streets they sacrificed to Baal.

why: The Hebrew has the shorter line. The Greek's extra words match the Hebrew of 11:13, so a Greek copyist could have carried them over from there; no Hebrew witness has them here.

a: You did not catch them tunneling in
p: The Greek says 'I did not find them in tunnels, but under every oak'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.orig: לֹא בַמַּחְתֶּרֶת מְצָאתִים כִּי עַל כָּל אֵלֶּה
readings.en: not in the tunnel did you find them, but on all these
readings.plain: You did not catch them tunneling in

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: οὐκ ἐν διορύγμασιν εὗρον αὐτοὺς ἀλλ᾽ ἐπὶ πάσῃ δρυί
readings.en: not in tunnels did I (or they) find them, but under every oak
readings.plain: I did not find them tunneling in, but under every oak

why: The Hebrew is hard, but it makes a clear point about Exodus 22:2-3 (see the note). The Greek seems to have read 'elleh' ('these') as a word like 'elah' ('oak, terebinth') and its verb can be 'I found'. The Hebrew pointing has 'you found'. Neither fits the line well, so the Plain English keeps the Hebrew. The Greek also has 'in your hands' for 'on your skirts'. No scroll preserves 2:34.
b: If the Greek is followed, the next line of the Plain, 'But there is all of this', no longer fits and would be dropped.

a: Can he go back to her again?
p: The Hebrew asks whether the husband will return; the Greek asks whether the wife will.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); the sense of Deuteronomy 24:4
readings.en: Can he return to her again?
readings.plain: Can he go back to her again?

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: μὴ ἀνακάμπτουσα ἀνακάμψει πρὸς αὐτὸν ἔτι;
readings.en: Will she, returning, return to him again?
readings.plain: Can she go back to him again?

why: Deuteronomy 24:4 forbids the first husband to take the wife back, which is the law Jeremiah is using. The Greek has the wife returning, and goes with the next lines in a different way (below).
b: No scroll preserves 3:1. The Hebrew line is the ordinary question hayashuv, 'will he return?'. The Greek's wife as subject would need a feminine verb (tashuv) in its Hebrew; no Hebrew witness has it.

a: Would that land not be completely polluted?
p: The Greek says the woman, not the land, is made unclean.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: Would not that land be utterly polluted?
readings.plain: Would that land not be completely polluted?

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: οὐ μιαινομένη μιανθήσεται ἡ γυνὴ ἐκείνη;
readings.en: Will not that woman be utterly defiled?
readings.plain: Would that woman not be completely polluted?

why: Deuteronomy 24:4 says the return would 'bring sin on the land', which is the Hebrew's wording. The Greek may have changed it to match the picture of a woman.

a: Yet return to me
p: The Hebrew can be read as a command, 'Yet return to me!', or as a question, 'Would you return to me?'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), the infinitive absolute veshov read as a command; so Rashi (the LORD's longing) and the Latin Vulgate (an imperative, as printed at Bible Gateway)
readings.en: Yet return to me!
readings.plain: Yet return to me

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.en: And were you returning to me?
readings.plain: And would you return to me?

why: The Hebrew verb is an infinitive absolute, which can carry the force of a command, and that fits the LORD's repeated call to turn back (3:12, 14, 22). Rashi says the word means 'and to return to me' and hears the LORD's longing. The Greek ('And were you returning to me?') and the revised Jewish Publication Society translation (2023, 'can you return to Me?') take it as a question. A question makes the line a rebuke; a command makes it an invitation.
b: No scroll preserves this verse. Commentators and versions divide as described above; the Plain English follows the command because 3:12-14 repeats the call.

a: with many companions
p: The Greek has the woman acting as a prostitute 'among many shepherds'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: with many companions
readings.plain: with many companions

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.en: with many shepherds
readings.plain: with many shepherds

why: The Hebrew re'im, 'companions' (lovers), and ro'im, 'shepherds', have the same letters. 'Companions' fits the rest of the picture (2:25; 4:30). The Greek's 'shepherds' (rulers) looks like another way of pointing the same word, and it uses it again in 3:3. No scroll preserves 3:1.

a: been lain with
p: The margin has the mild 'lain with'; the written text has 'ravished'.

readings.w: Qere (read) of the Leningrad Codex
readings.en: you have been lain with
readings.plain: been lain with

readings.w: Ketiv (written) of the Leningrad Codex
readings.en: you have been ravished
readings.plain: been ravished

why: The Masoretes read a milder verb in place of the blunt written one, as they do at Deuteronomy 28:30, Isaiah 13:16 and Zechariah 14:2. The sense of the line is the same. The Plain English follows the pointed text. No scroll preserves 3:2.

a: like a nomad in the wilderness
p: The Hebrew has 'like an Arab'; the Greek has 'like a crow'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: like an Arab in the wilderness
readings.plain: like a nomad in the wilderness

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.en: like a crow left alone
readings.plain: like a crow in the wilderness

why: The Hebrew words for 'Arab' and for 'raven or crow' ('orev) have almost the same letters. The Hebrew picture, a herder waiting by the road to waylay travelers, fits 'sat waiting' better than a bird does. No scroll preserves 3:2.

a: So the showers were held back,
t: The showers are not in the Greek
p: The Greek has no line about the showers; it has 'many shepherds' here. It goes with the next entry.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and the showers were held back
readings.plain: So the showers were held back,

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: καὶ ἔσχες ποιμένας πολλοὺς εἰς πρόσκομμα σεαυτῇ
readings.en: and you had many shepherds as a stumbling block to yourself
readings.plain: You had many shepherds as a stumbling block to yourself,

why: The Hebrew rain-curse (Deuteronomy 11:16-17) is the covenant penalty and ties into 14:1-6. The Greek instead repeats the 'shepherds' of its 3:1, so its line may come from a reading of the Hebrew like the one in the entry at 3:1. No scroll preserves 3:3.

a: and no spring rain came.
t: The spring rain is not in the Greek
p: The Greek has no 'no spring rain'; it goes with the entry before.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and spring rain did not come
readings.plain: and no spring rain came.

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.en: (omitted)

why: The Greek's 3:3 has one line where the Hebrew has the showers and the spring rain, and then the prostitute's forehead. No scroll preserves 3:3.

a: She will return to me
p: The Greek has the LORD say 'Return to me'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: to me she will return
readings.plain: She will return to me

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.en: Return to me
readings.plain: Return to me

why: In the Hebrew the LORD hopes for her return and is disappointed; in the Greek he tells her to return and she does not. The Hebrew word for 'she will return' and a command like 'return!' (shuvi) are close, so one may have changed into the other. No scroll preserves 3:7.

a: The ark of the covenant of the LORD.
t: 'Of the LORD' or 'of the Holy One of Israel'?
p: The Greek names the ark as 'of the Holy One of Israel'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: The ark of the covenant of the LORD
readings.plain: The ark of the covenant of the LORD.

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.en: The ark of the covenant of the Holy One of Israel
readings.plain: The ark of the covenant of the Holy One of Israel.

why: The Hebrew has the usual title. The Greek is probably a translator's variation (compare Isaiah's 'Holy One of Israel'), since no Hebrew witness has it; but a different Hebrew text is possible.

a: , to the name of the LORD, to Jerusalem
t: 'To the name of the LORD' is not in the Greek
p: The Greek stops at 'all the nations will gather to it'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: to the name of the LORD, to Jerusalem
readings.plain: , to the name of the LORD, to Jerusalem

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.en: (omitted)

why: The longer Hebrew repeats 'Jerusalem' in a way the Greek has not. No scroll preserves the verse, so the question stays open; it is one of the places where the Hebrew may have grown.

a: I said to myself,
p: The Greek has someone answer 'So be it, Lord' and goes on differently from there.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and I said: how I will set you among the sons
readings.plain: I said to myself,

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: καὶ ἐγὼ εἶπα Γένοιτο, Κύριε· ὅτι τάξω σε εἰς ἔθνη, καὶ δώσω σοι γῆν ἐκλεκτὴν κληρονομίαν θεοῦ Παντοκράτορος ἐθνῶν
readings.en: and I said, So be it, Lord, for I will set you among the nations, and give you a chosen land, an inheritance of God Almighty of the nations
readings.plain: I said, "So be it, Lord.

why: The Hebrew has the LORD recalling his own hope, 'how I will set you among the sons'. The Greek has a reply, 'So be it, Lord', and reads 'nations' for 'sons' (perhaps goyim for banim) and, perhaps, 'God Almighty' for 'beauty of beauties'. The two texts tell the story differently from here to the end of the verse, so the switched wording shown above is only the start of the Greek line. No scroll preserves 3:19.

a: from my sight
t: From my sight, or from his mouth?
p: The Greek speaks of Israel's 'mouth' in the third person.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: from before me
readings.plain: from my sight

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition): 'If Israel turns to me, he will turn; if he removes his abominations from his mouth ...'
readings.en: from his mouth
readings.plain: from his mouth

why: The Hebrew speaks to Israel directly; the Greek has Israel in the third person and 'mouth' for 'before me', which may be a misreading of a similar Hebrew word, or another text. No scroll preserves 4:1-2 (4QJer-c begins at 4:5).

a: and do not wander,
t: 'Do not wander' or 'be careful before me'?
p: The Greek has the verb 'be careful, reverent' for the Hebrew 'do not wander'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and do not wander
readings.plain: and do not wander,

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.en: and is wary of my face
readings.plain: and show reverence before my face,

why: The Hebrew has an easy sense, to waver or wander, which fits the picture of Israel's unfaithfulness. The Greek has a different verb and no negative; whether a different Hebrew lies behind it is unknown.

a: and in him they will boast.
p: The Greek makes the nations praise God 'in Jerusalem'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and in him they will boast
readings.plain: and in him they will boast.

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ αἰνέσουσιν τῷ θεῷ ἐν Ἰερουσαλήμ
readings.en: and in him they will praise God in Jerusalem
readings.plain: and in him they will praise God in Jerusalem.

why: The Hebrew is the shorter, more usual wording. The Greek adds 'in Jerusalem', which may come from a Greek translator's expansion or from a different Hebrew; no scroll preserves the verse.

a: A scorching wind from the bare hills in the wilderness
t: A hot wind or a spirit of error?
p: The Greek says 'a spirit of error in the wilderness'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: a hot wind from the bare heights in the wilderness
readings.plain: A scorching wind from the bare hills in the wilderness

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.en: A spirit of error in the wilderness
readings.plain: A spirit of leading astray in the wilderness

why: The Hebrew is clear and fits the winnowing image that follows. The Greek translated ruach as 'spirit' and may have read a different word for 'hot' and 'bare heights'. 4QJer-c does not preserve this verse.

a: I am writhing.
p: The written text and the Greek say 'I am in pain'; the marginal reading says 'I wait'.

readings.w: Ketiv (written) of the Leningrad Codex; Greek ('I am in pain'); Latin Vulgate ('doleo') as reported by commentaries
readings.en: I writhe
readings.plain: I am writhing.

readings.w: Qere (read) of the Leningrad Codex
readings.en: I wait
readings.plain: I am waiting.

why: 'I wait' does not suit a cry of pain. The pain reading is supported by the written text and the Greek. No scroll preserves 4:19 (4QJer-c ends at 4:16 in what survives).

a: For you have heard, my soul,
p: The Qere has 'you have heard'; the written text has 'I have heard'; the Greek 'my soul has heard'.

readings.w: Qere (read) of the Leningrad Codex
readings.en: you have heard, my soul
readings.plain: For you have heard, my soul,

readings.w: Ketiv (written) of the Leningrad Codex
readings.en: I have heard, my soul
readings.plain: For I have heard, my soul,

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.en: my soul has heard
readings.plain: For my soul has heard

why: The two Ketiv/Qere pairs in this verse are judged one by one. 'I wait' (Qere) does not suit a cry of pain, so the first word follows the written text and the Greek. For the second, the Plain English keeps the Qere, 'you have heard', because it puts 'my soul' in direct address, as the speaker talking to himself (compare Psalm 42:5). The Ketiv, 'I have heard, my soul', is possible too. The Greek, 'my soul has heard', agrees with neither in person. So the verse has 'I writhe' and 'you have heard': a person speaking to his own soul, and the person changes in the speech.

a: gathered in crowds at a prostitute's house
p: One Hebrew verb, read two ways, and a Greek verb that means 'stayed overnight'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), understood as 'gathered in troops'
readings.en: and in a prostitute's house they gathered in crowds
readings.plain: gathered in crowds at a prostitute's house

readings.w: The same Hebrew word, understood as 'cut themselves' (as of cult mourning)
readings.en: they cut gashes in themselves at a prostitute's house
readings.plain: cut gashes in themselves at a prostitute's house

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.en: in the houses of prostitutes they lodged
readings.plain: stayed overnight in prostitutes' houses

b: The Hebrew yitgodadu can come from a root for a raiding troop, so 'gathered in crowds', or from a root meaning to cut, as in the cult mourning of 1 Kings 18:28 and Jeremiah 16:6; 41:5; 47:5.
why: The same verb is used elsewhere for gathering in bands (Micah 5:1), and the context is adultery, not mourning. The Greek 'lodged' is a different verb and may point to a different Hebrew word. No scroll preserves 5:7.

a: a nation that has lasted, a nation from ancient times,
t: 'An enduring nation, an ancient nation' is missing in the Greek
p: The Greek omits two descriptions of the invader.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.orig: גוֹי אֵיתָן הוּא גּוֹי מֵעוֹלָם הוּא
readings.en: it is an enduring nation, it is an ancient nation
readings.plain: a nation that has lasted, a nation from ancient times,

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.en: (omitted)

a: a well
p: The margin has 'well'; the written text and the Greek have 'cistern'.

readings.w: Qere (read) of the Leningrad Codex
readings.en: a well
readings.plain: a well

readings.w: Ketiv (written) of the Leningrad Codex; Greek (lakkos, 'cistern, pit')
readings.en: a cistern
readings.plain: a cistern

why: The sense is the same: a water store. The Plain English keeps the margin's 'well' as the pointed text. The Greek's line, 'as a cistern keeps cool its water, so she keeps cool her evil', also supports the 'keeps fresh' sense of the verb (see the note). No scroll preserves 6:7.

a: you will find rest for yourselves
p: The Hebrew promises 'rest for your souls'; the Greek 'purification for your souls'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); quoted in Matthew 11:29 ('rest for your souls')
readings.en: and find rest for your souls
readings.plain: you will find rest for yourselves

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.en: you will find purification for your souls
readings.plain: you will find purification for yourselves

why: 'Rest' (marge'a, a rare word, found only here and in Isaiah 28:12) is the Hebrew; Matthew's 'rest' (anapausin) agrees with it and not with this Greek. The Greek translator probably read a different word or chose a word of his own. No scroll preserves 6:16.

p: The margin has 'the lead is finished off by the fire'; the written text has 'from their fire'; the Greek differs.

readings.w: Greek Jeremiah (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete's edition)
readings.orig: ἐξέλιπεν φυσητὴρ ἀπὸ πυρός ἐξέλιπεν μόλιβος
readings.en: the bellows gave out in the fire; the lead gave out
readings.plain: the lead gives out

why: The written text, which runs two words together, is hard to make sense of; the margin divides it into 'from fire' and 'finished', which gives the picture of lead used up in the refining. The Greek line (the bellows and the lead give out, and 'in vain the silversmith smelts') is nearer to the margin's sense than to the written text. No scroll preserves 6:29.
